newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's economy making surprise year-end surge.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's economy making surprise year-end surge.

text.p: A slew of upbeat reports on the Mexican economy this week suggest that fourth quarter growth will be surprisingly strong and could mark the fastest sustained growth period in 15 years, economists said.

Industrial production, trade, retail sales and employment data released in the last week suggest that the economy could grow five percent in the fourth quarter compared with the same period last year.

In deseasonalized terms, or quarter-on-quarter, that would mark the longest sustained period of robust growth since 1980-1981, "when Mexico was in full oil boom," said Carlos Rosales, an economist at Bancomer.

It is a rebound that has not yet made it into the wallets of many Mexicans, and part of the strength is explained by the comparison with a nightmare recession last year in the aftermath of the December 1994 peso crisis.
But analysts say there are indications that it is becoming a recovery in the full sense of the word, with jobs growth, some wage recovery and the first hints of consumer spending.

In a Reuters survey, analysts recently forecast Q4 year-on-year growth at 4.72 percent. But they have under-estimated almost all the Q4 data released this week, and Rosales said five percent growth was "perfectly possible."

Industrial output in October rose 15.5 percent, well above the 10.65 percent average forecast. Unemployment in November fell to 4.8 percent, its lowest level in 22 months, as more than 500,000 people found work. A 5.1 percent rate had been forecast.

Retail sales in Mexico rose 2.1 percent in October, wheras analysts had predicted a 1.53 percent increase. And in revised October trade data released last week, both imports and exports surged, with consumer goods imports hitting $712 million, up 52.2 percent from October 1995, partly due to private spending.

"It is a rebound from an intense fall, but also the progress (in the economy) has been very rapid," an enthusiastic Rosales said, noting also that the recovery was what he called autonomous. "It is not being induced by the public sector."

Gray Newman, economist at HSBC James Capel, said he raised his Q4 GDP forecast to 5.5 percent as a result of the industrial production data. He expected activity to remain above the 13-14 percent range in November. He was more cautious about the employment situation, saying that much of the jobs growth in October was Christmas-driven and that such posts were liable to "evaporate" in January

"The problem with growth in Mexico is that it continues to be export-orientated. It provides very little employment. Most of the economy is in the service sector," he said, though he did acknowledge a "mild consumer recovery is taking place."
For Enrique Ramirez, economist at Santander Investments, growth could top five percent in the fourth quarter if industrial production continued to hum at a 10-11 percent level in November.
He also sees a coming spending recovery, fueled by jobs growth and a rise in the minimum wage in December, that he said was reflected in the import surge reported in the trade data.
"The rise in the minimum wage could improve wages as a whole in the coming months, which is going to cause a rise in consumption," he said.
